questions.q: Why is a root cause from an after-action report "only half-useful" until it becomes a detection?
options: Root causes are legally required to be deleted after the report is filed
After-action reports are never accurate enough to act on
Sentinel cannot accept any input based on a written document
A root cause that only lives in a document relies on a human noticing the same pattern again, instead of being caught automatically
questions.explain: Turning the root cause into an analytics rule means the same pattern is flagged automatically next time, not just documented.

questions.q: Which table does this lesson's detection query use, and where does it come from?
options: AuditLogs, which tracks only administrative role changes
DeviceProcessEvents, the Microsoft Defender for Endpoint process table available in Sentinel via the Defender XDR connector
SigninLogs, the Microsoft Entra ID sign-in table
A table that must be manually created from scratch with no real source
questions.explain: DeviceProcessEvents is the Defender for Endpoint process table, the same kind of real table Chapter 3 built queries against.

questions.q: Why was the first-pass query filtering only on schtasks.exe with /create too broad to use as a rule?
options: KQL does not support filtering on command-line arguments
Legitimate software and IT admins create scheduled tasks constantly, so it would generate excessive noise
Scheduled tasks can only be created by attackers, so this isn't a real concern
schtasks.exe never actually appears in DeviceProcessEvents
questions.explain: Scheduled task creation is routine for legitimate software, so the base query alone would bury the SOC in false positives.

questions.q: What specific detail narrowed the query into a precise, low-noise detection?
options: Checking the time zone the server was configured with
Removing the FileName filter entirely
Checking the exact username of every administrator
Checking whether the scheduled task's command line pointed to AppData, Temp, or a public user folder — not where legitimate software typically launches from
questions.explain: has_any ("\\AppData\\", "\\Temp\\", "\\Users\\Public\\") targets the specific suspicious launch locations from the actual incident.

questions.q: Once the finished query is pasted into a Scheduled Analytics Rule, what makes it a real, usable detection rather than just a query?
options: Renaming the query file to end in .rule
Nothing further is needed — any KQL query is automatically a rule
A run frequency and lookback window, an alert threshold, and entity mapping of DeviceName and AccountName to trackable entities
Running it manually once a year during an audit
questions.explain: Scheduling, threshold, and entity mapping are what turn a KQL query into a running analytics rule that produces trackable incidents.
